laws.title: Speed Limits — StVO (Baden-Württemberg)
laws.subtitle: Built-up: 50km/h; rural: 100km/h; Autobahn: advisory 130km/h
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg follows Germany's federal StVO. Urban areas: 50km/h. Rural roads: 100km/h. Autobahn: no general limit but advisory 130km/h. Tempo-30 zones are widespread in residential areas across cities like Stuttgart, Freiburg, and Heidelberg. Running out of fuel on the Autobahn is illegal. The state has extensive Autobahn network (A5, A6, A7, A8, A81).
laws.penalty: Exceeding limit by 20km/h in town: €70 + 1 point. 31km/h+ over: €200 + 1 point + 1-month ban.
laws.exceptions: Autobahn sections with variable gantry signs override advisory limit

quiz.q: What is the advisory speed on Germany's unrestricted Autobahn sections?
quiz.explanation: The advisory (Richtgeschwindigkeit) on unrestricted Autobahn is 130 km/h — not legally binding but relevant to liability in accidents.

laws.title: Drink-Driving — BAC Limits (StVG §24a)
laws.subtitle: 0.5‰ general limit; 0.0‰ for new drivers and under-21s
laws.fullDescription: Germany sets a 0.5‰ BAC limit for general drivers. Drivers with less than 2 years' licence or under 21 face a strict 0.0‰ limit. At 1.6‰ or above, a mandatory medical-psychological assessment (MPU — 'idiot test') is required before licence reinstatement. Baden-Württemberg police conduct regular roadside checks on B-roads and near Stuttgart's nightlife areas.
laws.penalty: 0.5–0.79‰: €500 fine + 1 month ban + 2 points. 0.8‰+: criminal offence, up to 5 years prison. 0.0‰ violation for new drivers: €250 + 1 point.
laws.exceptions: Emergency medical transport

quiz.q: What BAC limit applies to drivers with less than 2 years' licence in Germany?
quiz.explanation: Germany imposes an absolute 0.0‰ limit on novice drivers (licence under 2 years) and those under 21, to reduce accident risk during the most dangerous period of driving.

laws.title: Mobile Phone While Driving — §23 StVO
laws.subtitle: Handheld device use banned; hands-free required
laws.fullDescription: Using a handheld mobile phone or any electronic device while driving or cycling is prohibited under §23 StVO. Hands-free operation is permitted if the device doesn't need to be picked up. Baden-Württemberg has heavy traffic enforcement especially on Stuttgart's ring roads. Even holding a phone at a red light counts as an offence.
laws.penalty: €100 fine + 1 point. With accident caused: €150–€200 + possible criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Hands-free calls with mounted device

quiz.q: Can you use your phone at a red light in Germany?
options: No — holding a phone while driving (including at lights) is illegal
quiz.explanation: Holding a phone at a red light counts as a §23 StVO violation in Germany — the car must be parked with the engine off for phone use to be legal.

laws.title: Cycling Laws — Radwegebenutzungspflicht
laws.subtitle: Designated cycle paths must be used where signed
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg has extensive cycle infrastructure. Where a cycle path is signed with a blue bicycle symbol (Zeichen 237), cyclists must use it — not the road. Cycling on pavements is illegal except where explicitly marked. Cyclists must use lights after dark (front white, rear red) and audible bells are mandatory. Alcohol limit for cyclists is 1.6‰ (criminal), though 0.0‰ applies to under-21s.
laws.penalty: Cycling without lights: €20. Wrong side of road: €15. No bell: €15. Drunk cycling (1.6‰+): criminal prosecution, licence at risk.
laws.exceptions: Shared pavement zones (Zeichen 239 + bicycle symbol) permit pavement cycling

quiz.q: What BAC level makes cycling a criminal offence in Germany?
quiz.explanation: Cycling becomes a criminal offence at 1.6‰ BAC in Germany — the same threshold that triggers a mandatory MPU psychological test for drivers.

laws.title: Ruhezeiten — Quiet Hours (Baden-Württemberg)
laws.subtitle: Nightly 22:00–06:00; Sundays all day; midday 13:00–15:00 in some areas
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg's Landesimmissionsschutzgesetz establishes strict quiet hours: 22:00–06:00 daily, all-day Sundays and public holidays. Some municipalities (especially Freiburg and Tübingen) add a midday Mittagsruhe from 13:00–15:00. Lawnmowers, power tools, loud music, and domestic appliances on high spin are all covered. Baden-Württemberg has 12 official public holidays — one of the highest in Germany — expanding Sunday-equivalent quiet days significantly.
laws.penalty: Violations: €500–€5,000. Persistent breach: civil action by neighbours.
laws.exceptions: Emergency repairs with police notification

quiz.q: Baden-Württemberg has how many official public holidays — one of Germany's highest counts?
quiz.explanation: Baden-Württemberg has 12 official public holidays, including Catholic-specific days like Epiphany (Jan 6), Corpus Christi, and All Saints Day — reflecting the state's historically Catholic south.

laws.title: Pfand — Bottle Deposit System (VerpackG)
laws.subtitle: 25-cent mandatory deposit on plastic/glass bottles and cans
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Pfand (deposit) system under the Verpackungsgesetz requires a 25-cent deposit on most plastic and glass bottles and aluminium cans. Bottles are returned at supermarket Pfandautomaten. Baden-Württemberg has a strong environmental culture — Freiburg im Breisgau is considered Germany's 'Green City' and pioneered solar energy adoption. Mulltrennung (waste separation) is mandatory: Papier (blue), Gelber Sack (yellow — packaging), Biomüll (brown — organic), Restmüll (grey — general).
laws.penalty: Retailers failing to accept returns: heavy fines. Non-separated waste may be refused collection.
laws.exceptions: Wine bottles, milk cartons, juice boxes often exempt (Mehrwegsystem varies)

quiz.q: Which German city is nicknamed the 'Green City' and pioneered solar energy adoption?
quiz.explanation: Freiburg im Breisgau in Baden-Württemberg is Germany's 'Green City' — it has Europe's highest solar energy per capita, extensive tram networks, and a culture of environmental activism dating to the 1970s anti-nuclear movement.

laws.title: Mietrecht — Tenant Rights (BGB §535ff)
laws.subtitle: Strong tenant protections; notice periods; deposit rules
laws.fullDescription: German tenancy law (BGB §535ff) provides some of the world's strongest tenant protections. Landlords must give 3–9 months' notice for ordinary termination (longer for longer tenancies). Security deposits are capped at 3 months' cold rent. Baden-Württemberg cities like Stuttgart and Heidelberg have acute housing shortages — Stuttgart has Germany's highest ratio of income spent on rent outside Berlin/Munich. The Mietpreisbremse (rent brake) applies in designated high-demand areas across the state.
laws.penalty: Illegal eviction: criminal prosecution. Deposit withholding without reason: court order for return + interest.
laws.exceptions: Landlords may terminate for own use (Eigenbedarf) with documented need

quiz.q: How many months of cold rent can a German landlord require as security deposit?
quiz.explanation: German law caps residential tenancy security deposits at 3 months' Kaltmiete (cold rent, excluding utilities) — protecting tenants from excessive upfront costs.

laws.title: Cannabis — Cannabisgesetz 2024 (Baden-Württemberg)
laws.subtitle: Adults 18+: 25g public, 50g home, 3 plants legal
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Cannabis Act (CanG) effective April 2024 legalised recreational cannabis. Adults 18+ may possess up to 25g in public, 50g at home, and cultivate up to 3 plants. Cannabis social clubs (up to 500 members) may collectively grow. Baden-Württemberg's CDU-led state government opposed the law but must enforce it. No commercial cannabis shops exist yet — sales are via clubs only. Consumption near schools, playgrounds, and pedestrian zones is prohibited. The 200m exclusion zone around schools is actively enforced.
laws.penalty: Under-18 possession: fines + youth support measures. Over-limit: fines up to €30,000. Sales outside clubs: criminal prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Medical cannabis has separate prescription framework

quiz.q: How much cannabis can an adult legally possess in public in Germany?
quiz.explanation: Germany's 2024 Cannabis Act (CanG) permits adults to carry up to 25 grams in public and keep up to 50 grams at home — making Germany one of the EU's most permissive cannabis regimes.

laws.title: Weapons Law — Waffengesetz (WaffG)
laws.subtitle: Germany has strict firearms licensing; most weapons require Waffenbesitzkarte
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Weapons Act (WaffG) classifies weapons into prohibited (Anlage 2), restricted (licence required), and free (no licence). To own a firearm, most people need a Waffenbesitzkarte (possession card) — requiring background check, safe storage, and legitimate purpose (hunting/sport/collection). Carrying loaded weapons requires an Ausnahmegenehmigung. Baden-Württemberg has a strong hunting culture — the Jagdschein (hunting licence) entitles holders to carry hunting rifles in the field.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed firearm possession: up to 3 years. Illegal carrying: up to 5 years. Prohibited weapons (automatic, silencers): up to 5 years.
laws.exceptions: Hunters with valid Jagdschein; licensed sports shooters; collectors with WBK

quiz.q: What document does a German hunter need to legally carry a rifle in the field?
quiz.explanation: A valid Jagdschein (hunting licence) in Germany entitles the holder to carry hunting firearms in the field during the hunt — it serves as both a firearms and hunting authorisation.

laws.title: Mindestlohn — National Minimum Wage (MiLoG)
laws.subtitle: €12.41/hour (2024), rising annually
laws.fullDescription: Germany introduced its first national minimum wage in 2015 under the Mindestlohngesetz (MiLoG). As of 2024, the rate is €12.41/hour gross — one of the EU's highest. The Mindestlohnkommission reviews it every 2 years. Baden-Württemberg has above-average wages due to its automotive and engineering industries (Daimler, Bosch, Porsche, SAP). Apprentices (Azubis) have a separate minimum under the Berufsbildungsgesetz (€620/month first year).
laws.penalty: Violations: fines up to €500,000 (employers). Record-keeping failures for documentation of working hours: up to €30,000.
laws.exceptions: Genuinely self-employed (Freiberufler) excluded; some internships exempt

quiz.q: What year did Germany introduce its first national minimum wage?
quiz.explanation: Germany introduced its first ever national minimum wage of €8.50/hour in January 2015 under the Mindestlohngesetz — relatively late compared to most EU countries.

laws.title: Working Hours — Arbeitszeitgesetz (ArbZG)
laws.subtitle: Max 8h/day; up to 10h with compensation; 11h rest minimum
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Working Hours Act (ArbZG) sets the standard working day at 8 hours, extensible to 10 hours if the average over 6 months doesn't exceed 8 hours. Minimum rest between shifts: 11 hours. Sunday work requires special permission. Baden-Württemberg's automotive sector (Daimler, Porsche) uses collective bargaining agreements (Tarifverträge) negotiated with IG Metall that often provide better terms than statutory minimums. The 35-hour week (IG Metall demand) applies in some sectors.
laws.penalty: Violations by employers: up to €15,000 fine. Repeat violations: criminal prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Emergency services, agriculture, seasonal industries have modified rules

quiz.q: What is the minimum rest period between shifts required under Germany's ArbZG?
quiz.explanation: Germany's ArbZG requires a minimum 11-hour rest period between the end of one shift and the start of the next — ensuring workers get adequate recovery time.

laws.title: DSGVO/GDPR Data Protection (Baden-Württemberg)
laws.subtitle: Germany has Europe's strictest data protection; state has its own LfDI
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg has its own state Data Protection Authority (LfDI — Landesbeauftragter für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit) that enforces GDPR (DSGVO in German) and the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG). The LfDI Stuttgart has fined companies for employee monitoring, CCTV overreach, and website cookie violations. Germany's constitutional right to 'informational self-determination' (Volkszählungsurteil 1983) underpins these protections. Companies processing personal data must have a documented legal basis.
laws.penalty: GDPR violations: up to €20 million or 4% of global turnover. German BDSG additions: further administrative fines.
laws.exceptions: Research, journalism, and public interest processing have documented exceptions

quiz.q: What constitutional right did Germany's 1983 census judgment establish?
quiz.explanation: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court's 1983 Volkszählungsurteil (census judgment) established the constitutional right to informational self-determination — the right to control data about oneself, forming the philosophical basis of European data protection law.

laws.title: Kirchensteuer — Church Tax (Baden-Württemberg)
laws.subtitle: 8% of income tax for registered Catholics/Protestants
laws.fullDescription: Germany automatically collects Kirchensteuer (church tax) from registered members of Catholic and Protestant churches via the income tax system. In Baden-Württemberg, the rate is 8% of income tax (not 8% of income). The state has a historically Catholic south (e.g., Rottenburg Diocese) and Protestant north. Leaving the church (Kirchenaustritt) requires a formal declaration at the Standesamt — it is not sufficient to simply stop attending. Many people leave to avoid this tax.
laws.penalty: Failure to declare membership change: back-tax liability. Fraudulent non-declaration: tax fraud prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Non-registered citizens and non-Christians pay no church tax

quiz.q: What is the Kirchensteuer rate in Baden-Württemberg?
quiz.explanation: Baden-Württemberg charges Kirchensteuer at 8% of the income tax owed (not 8% of gross income). Bavaria also charges 8%, while most other states charge 9%. The tax only applies to registered church members.

laws.title: Schulpflicht — Compulsory Education (Baden-Württemberg)
laws.subtitle: 9 years full-time + 3 years part-time (Berufsschule) compulsory
laws.fullDescription: Germany has some of the world's strictest compulsory schooling laws. Baden-Württemberg requires 9 years of full-time schooling, typically starting at age 6. Homeschooling (Hausunterricht) is illegal for school-age children — parents face fines, and in extreme cases children may be removed from the home. After full-time schooling, apprentices must attend Berufsschule (vocational school) part-time for up to 3 years. Baden-Württemberg's education system channels students into Hauptschule, Realschule, or Gymnasium at age 10 — one of Germany's most selective systems.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance by parents: fines up to €1,000; school truancy officers (Schulpflichtwächter) enforce attendance. Repeat violations: potential custody review.
laws.exceptions: Children with severe disabilities may have adapted schooling plans

quiz.q: Is homeschooling legal in Germany?
quiz.explanation: Homeschooling is illegal in Germany — all school-age children must attend accredited schools. This is one of the strictest homeschooling bans in the developed world, upheld by Germany's Constitutional Court in 2006.

laws.title: Krankenversicherungspflicht — Mandatory Health Insurance
laws.subtitle: All residents must have health insurance (GKV or PKV)
laws.fullDescription: Germany requires every resident to have health insurance — either statutory (GKV — Gesetzliche Krankenversicherung) or private (PKV — Private Krankenversicherung). Employees earning under the Versicherungspflichtgrenze (~€69,300/year in 2024) must join GKV. Self-employed and higher earners may choose PKV. Contributions for GKV are ~14.6% of gross salary (split employer/employee). Baden-Württemberg is home to major health insurers including AOK Baden-Württemberg and BW-Bank health plans.
laws.penalty: Uninsured periods create a back-payment obligation for all missed premiums when re-enrolling. Remaining uninsured is technically an administrative offence.
laws.exceptions: EU citizens with valid EHIC card have temporary coverage

quiz.q: What salary threshold generally determines whether a German employee must use statutory health insurance?
quiz.explanation: The Versicherungspflichtgrenze (compulsory insurance threshold) in Germany is approximately €69,300/year (2024). Employees earning above this can choose between GKV and PKV; below it, GKV membership is compulsory.

laws.title: Rundfunkbeitrag — Broadcasting Licence Fee
laws.subtitle: €18.36/month per household regardless of device ownership
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Rundfunkbeitrag is a compulsory household broadcasting fee of €18.36/month (2024), collected regardless of whether residents own a TV, radio, or streaming subscription. It funds ARD, ZDF, and Deutschlandradio public broadcasters. Baden-Württemberg contributes to the SWR (Südwestrundfunk) regional broadcaster. The fee is collected by Beitragsservice (formerly GEZ) and confirmed by all 16 state parliaments. Attempts to reduce it have been blocked by state parliaments, notably in Sachsen-Anhalt in 2020.
laws.penalty: Non-payment: reminders + fee increase + Inkasso (debt collection). Persistent refusal: enforcement by Vollstreckung. Fraudulent under-declaration: back-payments.
laws.exceptions: Low-income recipients of Bürgergeld/Sozialhilfe; severely disabled persons; students in shared accommodation (one fee per household)

quiz.q: What is Germany's monthly household broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag)?
quiz.explanation: Germany's Rundfunkbeitrag is €18.36/month per household (2024). It is a universal household fee — not linked to TV ownership — funding public broadcasters ARD, ZDF, and regional stations like Baden-Württemberg's SWR.

laws.title: Holocaust Denial and Nazi Symbols — §86a/§130 StGB
laws.subtitle: Displaying Nazi symbols or denying the Holocaust: up to 5 years
laws.fullDescription: Under StGB §86a, displaying symbols of unconstitutional organisations (swastika, SS runes, Heil Hitler salute, Nazi flags) in public is criminal — up to 3 years or a fine. §130 (Volksverhetzung — incitement to hatred) covers Holocaust denial, approval, or minimisation — up to 5 years. These laws apply to tourists and foreigners in Germany. Baden-Württemberg — the birthplace of the Nazi party's early organisation — has historically sensitive enforcement. Art, education, journalism, and critical commentary are exempt.
laws.penalty: §86a violation: up to 3 years or fine. §130 Holocaust denial: up to 5 years. Both apply to foreign nationals.
laws.exceptions: Museums, education, journalism, and art with documented critical purpose

quiz.q: What is the German legal term for the offence of incitement to hatred, including Holocaust denial?
quiz.explanation: Volksverhetzung (§130 StGB) — literally 'incitement of the people' — covers Holocaust denial, antisemitic content, and incitement against ethnic or social groups. It carries up to 5 years imprisonment and applies to all persons, including tourists, in Germany.

laws.title: Black Forest Protection — Naturschutzgesetz BW
laws.subtitle: Schwarzwald: protected areas, logging bans, trail rules
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg contains much of the Black Forest (Schwarzwald) — a major protected landscape. The state's Naturschutzgesetz and federal BNatSchG regulate activities in Naturschutzgebiete (nature reserves) and Landschaftsschutzgebiete (landscape protection zones). In protected areas: picking plants, disturbing wildlife, lighting fires, and off-trail cycling are prohibited. The Schwarzwald National Park (since 2014) has the strictest protections — no hunting, no logging, rewilding only. Mountain biking is restricted to marked trails.
laws.penalty: Violating nature reserve rules: fines €100–€25,000. Illegal logging: criminal prosecution + restoration costs.
laws.exceptions: Scientific research with permits; traditional agricultural practices in some zones

quiz.q: What significant protected area was established in Baden-Württemberg's Black Forest in 2014?
options: Black Forest UNESCO World Heritage Site
quiz.explanation: The Schwarzwald Nationalpark was established in 2014 — Baden-Württemberg's first and Germany's southernmost national park, covering 10,062 hectares of old-growth forest with a strict non-intervention rewilding policy.

laws.title: Gewerbeanmeldung — Trade Registration (GewO)
laws.subtitle: All businesses must register with local Gewerbeamt
laws.fullDescription: Under Germany's Trade Code (Gewerbeordnung — GewO), any person starting a commercial business (Gewerbe) must register with the local Gewerbeamt within the Rathaus (town hall) before starting operations. Registration costs €15–€65. Certain professions (Freie Berufe — doctors, lawyers, architects) are exempt and register with professional chambers (Kammern) instead. Baden-Württemberg's IHK (Industrie- und Handelskammer) Stuttgart is one of Germany's largest chambers, serving over 130,000 member businesses.
laws.penalty: Operating without registration: fines up to €10,000. Non-registration after warning: forced business closure.
laws.exceptions: Freie Berufe (liberal professions) register with Berufskammern instead

quiz.q: What is the German term for the regulatory office where businesses must register?
quiz.explanation: The Gewerbeamt (trade office), located within the Rathaus (town hall) of each municipality, is where new businesses must register (Gewerbeanmeldung) before starting operations in Germany.

laws.title: Marriage Law — BGB §1303ff
laws.subtitle: Minimum age 18; no religious-only marriage legally valid
laws.fullDescription: Germany requires civil marriage (Standesamtliche Heirat) for legal validity — religious ceremonies are not legally recognised on their own. Both partners must be 18+ (exceptions for under-18 with family court approval were largely abolished in 2017 — courts may dissolve child marriages). Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 2017 (Ehe für alle). Name changes must be registered with the Standesamt. International marriages require additional documentation (Ehefähigkeitszeugnis from country of origin).
laws.penalty: Bigamy: criminal offence under §172 StGB, up to 3 years. Marriage fraud for residency: deportation + ban.
laws.exceptions: EU citizens from countries where marriage conditions differ may face additional procedural requirements

quiz.q: When did same-sex marriage become legal throughout Germany?
quiz.explanation: Germany legalised same-sex marriage (Ehe für alle — marriage for all) on 1 October 2017, following a free vote in the Bundestag where even Chancellor Merkel voted against but the majority voted in favour.

laws.title: Tierschutzgesetz — Animal Welfare Act
laws.subtitle: Dogs must be walked twice daily; hot car abandonment criminal
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Tierschutzgesetz (Animal Welfare Act) and the 2021 Tierschutz-Hundeverordnung (Dog Welfare Ordinance) require that dogs be walked at least twice daily for a total of at least one hour. Dogs may not be permanently tethered. Leaving any animal in conditions causing suffering is criminal. In Baden-Württemberg, some municipalities require dogs over certain sizes or specific breeds to complete a Wesenstest (temperament test) and wear a muzzle in public. Dog tax (Hundesteuer) is charged by municipalities and varies widely — Stuttgart charges €108/year per dog.
laws.penalty: Dog welfare violations: fines up to €25,000. Animal cruelty: up to 3 years imprisonment.
laws.exceptions: Working dogs (police, military, guide dogs) have different exercise requirements

quiz.q: How many times per day must dogs legally be taken outside in Germany under the 2021 ordinance?
quiz.explanation: Germany's 2021 Tierschutz-Hundeverordnung requires dogs to be taken outside at least twice daily for at least one hour total — making Germany one of the few countries with legally mandated minimum daily exercise requirements for pet dogs.

laws.title: Aufenthaltsrecht — Residence Law (AufenthG)
laws.subtitle: Non-EU nationals need Aufenthaltserlaubnis; various visa categories
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Residence Act (Aufenthaltsgesetz — AufenthG) governs the legal stay of non-EU nationals. EU citizens have automatic free movement rights. Non-EU nationals generally need an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (temporary residence permit) or Niederlassungserlaubnis (permanent residence). Baden-Württemberg's Ausländerbehörden (aliens authorities) in Stuttgart, Freiburg, and Mannheim process permits. The 2023 Skilled Worker Immigration Act (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz) introduced the Chancenkarte (opportunity card) — a points-based visa allowing job seekers to enter Germany.
laws.penalty: Overstaying a visa: deportation + re-entry ban. Working without permit: fines for employer (€500,000) and employee.
laws.exceptions: EU/EEA/Swiss citizens: free movement without permit requirement

quiz.q: What new visa type did Germany's 2023 Skilled Worker Immigration Act create?
quiz.explanation: The Chancenkarte (Opportunity Card) — introduced by Germany's 2023 Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz — is a points-based visa allowing skilled workers to enter Germany to search for employment without a prior job offer.

laws.title: Online Shopping — Widerrufsrecht (14-Day Return Right)
laws.subtitle: Consumers have 14-day unconditional right to return online purchases
laws.fullDescription: Under EU Directive 2011/83/EU and German BGB §355ff, consumers have an unconditional 14-day right to return goods purchased online, by phone, or door-to-door without giving reasons. The return period starts when goods are received. Sellers must clearly inform buyers of this right — failing to do so extends the return window to 12 months. Baden-Württemberg consumers can report non-compliant retailers to the Verbraucherzentrale Baden-Württemberg.
laws.penalty: Retailers denying the return right: consumer rights violations + Verbraucherschutz complaints. Fraudulent return of used goods: criminal fraud.
laws.exceptions: Perishable goods, customised products, sealed hygiene items once opened excluded
laws.sourceLabel: BGB §355ff — Widerrufsrecht / EU Consumer Rights Directive

quiz.q: How many days do German consumers have to return online purchases?
quiz.explanation: German law (BGB §355ff implementing EU Directive 2011/83) grants consumers a 14-day unconditional right to return goods purchased online, by phone, or at the door without giving any reason.

laws.title: Erbrecht — Inheritance Law (BGB §1922ff)
laws.subtitle: Forced heirship (Pflichtteil); inheritance tax varies by relationship
laws.fullDescription: German inheritance law (BGB §1922ff) provides Pflichtteil (forced share) rights — close relatives (children, spouse, parents in some cases) cannot be entirely disinherited. Pflichtteil equals 50% of the legal intestate share. Baden-Württemberg applies federal Erbschaftsteuergesetz rates: spouses inherit tax-free up to €500,000; children up to €400,000; further amounts taxed 7–50% depending on relationship. Inheritances must be accepted or rejected within 6 weeks — acceptance implies taking on debts.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent inheritance claims: criminal prosecution. Tax evasion on inheritance: back-tax + penalties.
laws.exceptions: Charities receive inheritance tax exemptions

quiz.q: What is Germany's Pflichtteil in inheritance law?
options: 50% of what the legal intestate share would be
quiz.explanation: Germany's Pflichtteil (forced heirship share) guarantees close relatives — especially children and spouses — a minimum of 50% of what they would have inherited under intestacy rules, even if they are left out of the will.

laws.title: Wahlrecht — Voting Rights (BWahlG / LWahlG BW)
laws.subtitle: Federal: 18+; EU residents vote in European elections; state elections 18+
laws.fullDescription: German citizens 18+ may vote in federal (Bundestagswahl) and state (Landtagswahl) elections. Baden-Württemberg holds Landtag elections every 5 years — the CDU/CSU-affiliated CDU has historically dominated but the Greens have led the state government since 2011 (with SPD, then CDU as junior partners). EU citizens resident in Baden-Württemberg may vote in European Parliament and local elections. Non-EU foreign nationals cannot vote. Postal voting (Briefwahl) is easy to obtain.
laws.penalty: Voter fraud: up to 5 years imprisonment. Electoral intimidation: criminal prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Baden-Württemberg does not allow 16-year-olds to vote in state elections (unlike some other Länder)

quiz.q: Which party has led Baden-Württemberg's state government since 2011?
quiz.explanation: Die Grünen (Greens) have led Baden-Württemberg since 2011 under Minister-President Winfried Kretschmann — the only Green minister-president in any German state, making it a political landmark in the historically conservative south.

laws.title: Winterreifenpflicht — Winter Tyre Requirement (StVO §2)
laws.subtitle: Winter tyres required in icy/snowy conditions — no calendar date rule
laws.fullDescription: Germany requires winter tyres (or all-season tyres with M+S marking) when road conditions are icy, snowy, or slushy — not based on a calendar date but on actual conditions. Baden-Württemberg's Black Forest and Swabian Alb areas regularly have winter conditions October–April. Summer tyres on icy roads: the driver is liable for any accidents and loses insurance protection. Tyre depth must be at least 1.6mm legally, but 4mm is recommended for winter safety.
laws.penalty: Driving on summer tyres in winter conditions: €60 fine + 1 point. Causing accident without appropriate tyres: full liability + potential criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: All-season tyres marked M+S are acceptable

quiz.q: Germany's winter tyre requirement is based on which factor?
quiz.explanation: Germany's winter tyre requirement (StVO §2) is condition-based not date-based — tyres must be appropriate for actual road conditions. The informal rule 'O to O' (Oktober to Ostern — October to Easter) is a guideline, not a law.

laws.title: Apothekenpflicht — Pharmacy-Only Medicines
laws.subtitle: Most medicines only available through licensed pharmacies
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Apothekenpflicht requires that most pharmaceutical products — including many medicines freely available OTC in other countries — be sold only through licensed Apotheken (pharmacies). This includes many antihistamines, stronger pain relievers, and all prescription drugs (verschreibungspflichtig). Baden-Württemberg has approximately 2,400 pharmacies. Online ordering from EU-licensed pharmacies is permitted for non-prescription medicines. Emergency dispensing after hours is rotated among pharmacies (Notdienst).
laws.penalty: Selling prescription medicines without licence: criminal prosecution. Illegal importation of controlled medicines: customs seizure + fines.
laws.exceptions: Online EU-licensed pharmacies may sell non-prescription medicines

quiz.q: What is the German term for the requirement that most medicines be sold only in licensed pharmacies?
quiz.explanation: Apothekenpflicht (pharmacy obligation) means that the vast majority of pharmaceutical products in Germany must be purchased from a licensed Apotheke — even many medicines freely sold in supermarkets in other EU countries.

laws.title: Renewable Energy — Energiewende (Baden-Württemberg)
laws.subtitle: BW targets 80% renewable electricity by 2030
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg's Klimaschutz- und Klimawandelanpassungsgesetz (KlimaG BW) commits the state to climate neutrality by 2040 — 5 years ahead of the federal target. The state mandates solar panels on new commercial buildings (Solarpflicht since 2022 — first in Germany) and since 2023 on new residential buildings too. Baden-Württemberg has the most wind energy potential in southern Germany. The Windenergieerlass regulates siting of turbines near forests and residential areas.
laws.penalty: Violation of solar installation mandate on new builds: fines up to €50,000. Grid connection delays by utilities: regulatory penalties.
laws.exceptions: Heritage-listed buildings have alternative compliance routes

quiz.q: Baden-Württemberg was the first German state to mandate solar panels on which type of new buildings?
quiz.explanation: Baden-Württemberg became Germany's first state to mandate rooftop solar on new commercial buildings in 2022, later extending the requirement to new residential builds from 2023 — ahead of similar federal legislation.

laws.title: Pedestrian Rules — Jaywalking §25 StVO
laws.subtitle: Crossing against red pedestrian signal: technically illegal
laws.fullDescription: Under §25 StVO, crossing a red pedestrian signal (rotes Ampelmännchen) is technically illegal in Germany — with fines of €5–€10 rarely enforced. However, the social pressure in Baden-Württemberg is intense: crossing against red, especially near children, triggers immediate verbal censure from bystanders. The green Ampelmännchen (originally a GDR design now used nationally) is culturally sacred. Baden-Württemberg's cities have advanced pedestrian signal systems — in Stuttgart, some signals have a countdown display.
laws.penalty: Fine of €5–€10 (rarely enforced). Social censure from bystanders is immediate and strong.
laws.exceptions: Crossing when traffic has fully cleared — informal tolerance varies by city

quiz.q: What is the colloquial term for the green walk signal figure used in Germany?
quiz.explanation: The Ampelmännchen (little traffic light man) is Germany's beloved pedestrian signal figure — originally designed for the GDR (East Germany) in 1961, it survived reunification and is now used across Germany and internationally as a design icon.

laws.title: Stalking — §238 StGB (Nachstellung)
laws.subtitle: Persistent unwanted following/contact: up to 3 years
laws.fullDescription: Germany's anti-stalking law (§238 StGB — Nachstellung) criminalises persistently following, contacting, watching, or using personal data to threaten a person. The law covers both physical and online stalking. In 2017, the law was strengthened to remove the requirement that victims prove severe lifestyle disruption — any persistent unwanted contact can now trigger prosecution. Baden-Württemberg's LKA (state criminal office) has a dedicated cyberstalking unit.
laws.penalty: Stalking: up to 3 years or fine. If victim's health is damaged or victim commits suicide: up to 10 years.
laws.exceptions: Single instances of unwanted contact generally don't meet the 'persistent' threshold

quiz.q: What change to Germany's stalking law was made in 2017?
options: The requirement to prove 'severe lifestyle disruption' was removed
quiz.explanation: Germany's 2017 reform of §238 StGB removed the previous requirement that victims demonstrate their lifestyle was severely disrupted — making it easier to prosecute stalking from first reported incidents rather than requiring repeated serious harm.

laws.title: Elterngeld — Parental Leave Allowance
laws.subtitle: 65–67% of prior net income; up to 14 months shared
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Elterngeld (parental leave benefit) pays 65–67% of the parent's prior net income (minimum €300, maximum €1,800/month) for up to 12 months, extendable to 14 months if both parents take at least 2 months each (Partnermonate). ElterngeldPlus allows halved payments over double the time. Baden-Württemberg's Familienministerium also offers state-level Landeserziehungsgeld for a further 2 years. Elternzeit (job-protected parental leave) can last up to 3 years total — the job is protected even if the employer is small.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent Elterngeld claims: repayment + prosecution. Employer terminating during Elternzeit: automatically unfair dismissal, reinstatement order.
laws.exceptions: Both parents can take leave simultaneously or consecutively

quiz.q: What is the minimum and maximum monthly Elterngeld payment in Germany?
quiz.explanation: Germany's Elterngeld pays a minimum of €300 and maximum of €1,800/month — covering 65–67% of prior net income. The minimum ensures low-income parents still receive meaningful support during parental leave.

laws.title: GmbH Formation — Gesellschaft mit beschränkter Haftung
laws.subtitle: Minimum €25,000 capital; limited liability company structure
laws.fullDescription: Germany's most common business structure is the GmbH (Gesellschaft mit beschränkter Haftung — limited liability company). Requirements: minimum share capital of €25,000 (€12,500 must be paid at registration); notarised articles of association (Gesellschaftsvertrag); registration in the Handelsregister. Baden-Württemberg's Handelsregister is maintained by the Amtsgerichte (local courts) in each district. An alternative is the UG (haftungsbeschränkt) — a mini-GmbH with as little as €1 capital, requiring 25% of annual profit to be retained until €25,000 is reached.
laws.penalty: Operating without registration: fines + personal liability. Fraudulent capital declaration: criminal prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Sole traders (Einzelkaufleute) and partnerships (GbR) have simpler registration

quiz.q: What is the minimum share capital required to form a GmbH in Germany?
quiz.explanation: A GmbH in Germany requires a minimum share capital of €25,000, of which at least €12,500 must be paid in cash at registration. For start-ups, the UG (haftungsbeschränkt) allows formation with as little as €1.

laws.title: Baugenehmigung — Building Permits (LBO BW)
laws.subtitle: All significant construction requires permit; strict zoning rules
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg's Landesbauordnung (LBO BW) requires a Baugenehmigung (building permit) for all significant construction, renovation, or change of use of buildings. Minor works (small garden sheds, internal renovations) may be genehmigungsfrei (permit-free) under specific conditions. Applications go to the Baurechtsamt of the Landratsamt or Stadtamt. Bebauungspläne (development plans) define permitted building heights, densities, uses, and setbacks in each area. Stuttgart's hillside terrain creates additional constraints.
laws.penalty: Building without permit: demolition order + fines up to €500,000. Unauthorised use change: enforcement notice.
laws.exceptions: Small structures under defined size thresholds may be verfahrensfrei (procedure-free)

quiz.q: What document defines permitted land uses and building parameters in a German municipality?
quiz.explanation: The Bebauungsplan (development/zoning plan) is the binding local plan in Germany that defines what can be built on each plot — specifying height limits, setbacks, permitted uses (residential, commercial, mixed), floor area ratios, and green space requirements.

laws.title: Gewährleistung — Statutory Warranty (BGB §434ff)
laws.subtitle: 2-year statutory warranty on new goods; 1 year on used goods
laws.fullDescription: German law provides a 2-year Gewährleistung (statutory warranty/right to cure) on new goods — separate from any commercial Garantie (manufacturer's warranty). If goods are defective at the time of delivery, the seller must repair or replace at no charge. In the first 12 months, the defect is presumed to have existed at delivery (reversed burden of proof). Baden-Württemberg consumers can seek assistance from the Verbraucherzentrale BW for warranty disputes. Online purchases have the same warranty rights as in-store.
laws.penalty: Sellers denying valid warranty claims: Verbraucherschutz complaints + civil courts. Fraudulent goods: criminal fraud.
laws.exceptions: Second-hand goods between private individuals: no statutory warranty (caveat emptor applies)

quiz.q: What is the statutory warranty period for new goods in Germany?
quiz.explanation: German law (BGB §434ff) provides a 2-year Gewährleistung on new goods. In the first year, defects are presumed to have existed at delivery — reversing the burden of proof so the seller must prove the item was fine when sold.

laws.title: Betrug — Fraud (§263 StGB)
laws.subtitle: Obtaining property by deception: up to 5 years (10 in severe cases)
laws.fullDescription: Germany's fraud law (§263 StGB — Betrug) covers obtaining financial advantage through deception. Particularly severe cases (besonders schwerer Fall) — large amounts, professional fraud rings, abuse of position — carry up to 10 years. Computer fraud (§263a), subsidy fraud (§264), and insurance fraud (§265) are separate offences with similar penalties. Baden-Württemberg's LKA Stuttgart has specialist cyber-fraud units following major cases in the automotive industry region.
laws.penalty: Simple fraud: up to 5 years or fine. Severe fraud (gang, large scale, exploitation of vulnerable): up to 10 years.
laws.exceptions: Honest mistakes and misunderstandings — intent (Vorsatz) is required

quiz.q: What is the maximum penalty for serious commercial fraud (besonders schwerer Fall) in Germany?
quiz.explanation: Besonders schwerer Betrug (particularly severe fraud — §263 StGB) carries a maximum of 10 years imprisonment. This applies when the fraud is carried out professionally, in a gang, or causes very large losses.

laws.title: Rettungsgasse — Emergency Vehicle Corridor (§11 StVO)
laws.subtitle: Motorway jam: mandatory emergency lane between leftmost and second lane
laws.fullDescription: Under §11(2) StVO, drivers on multi-lane motorways must form a Rettungsgasse (rescue lane) between the leftmost lane and the next lane to the right when traffic stops or barely moves. This allows emergency vehicles to reach accident scenes. The law was significantly strengthened in 2017 after incidents of emergency vehicles being blocked. Baden-Württemberg has some of Germany's busiest Autobahn stretches (A8 Stuttgart–Munich; A5 Karlsruhe–Basel).
laws.penalty: Failure to form: €200–€320 + 2 points. Driving through it: up to €320 + driving ban. Obstructing: up to €240.
laws.exceptions: Single-lane roads excluded; the rule applies to motorways and expressways only

quiz.q: On German motorways, where must drivers form the Rettungsgasse (emergency corridor)?
options: Between the leftmost and second-from-left lane
In the middle of the road
quiz.explanation: German law requires drivers to form the Rettungsgasse between the leftmost (fast) lane and the lane immediately to its right — creating a corridor that emergency vehicles can use on multi-lane motorways during traffic jams.

laws.title: Water Protection — Wassergesetz BW
laws.subtitle: Strict water quality standards; groundwater protection zones
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg's Wassergesetz (WG BW) and the federal Wasserhaushaltsgesetz (WHG) protect water bodies and groundwater. Water protection zones (Wasserschutzgebiete) are designated around drinking water sources — activities within these zones (farming, fuel storage, certain construction) are restricted. The state has the largest number of natural mineral spring sources in Germany. Lake Constance (Bodensee) is managed jointly with Bavaria, Austria, and Switzerland under special treaty arrangements.
laws.penalty: Polluting protected water zones: fines up to €100,000 + remediation costs. Criminal water pollution: up to 5 years.
laws.exceptions: Agricultural activities in outer protection zones may continue under strict conditions

quiz.q: Lake Constance (Bodensee) is managed under a special agreement between Germany and which other countries?
quiz.explanation: The Bodensee (Lake Constance) is managed under the International Water Protection Commission for Lake Constance (IGKB), a joint body of Germany (Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria), Austria, and Switzerland — requiring cross-border environmental coordination.

laws.title: Betriebsverfassung — Works Council (BetrVG)
laws.subtitle: Employees in firms 5+ may elect a Betriebsrat; co-determination rights
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Betriebsverfassungsgesetz (BetrVG) gives employees in firms with 5+ permanent staff the right to elect a Betriebsrat (works council). The works council has rights to information, consultation, and co-determination on working hours, workplace procedures, dismissals, and major business changes. In firms with 500+ employees, workers elect representatives to the Supervisory Board (Mitbestimmung). Baden-Württemberg's major manufacturers (Daimler, Bosch, Porsche) have powerful Betriebsräte that negotiate significant worker protections beyond legal minimums.
laws.penalty: Obstructing works council elections: criminal offence (§119 BetrVG). Dismissing employee for works council activity: automatically unfair dismissal.
laws.exceptions: Firms under 5 employees and freelancers are excluded from BetrVG

quiz.q: At how many employees does a German company qualify for mandatory works council election rights?
quiz.explanation: Germany's BetrVG gives employees the right to elect a Betriebsrat (works council) in any firm with 5 or more permanent employees — one of the lowest thresholds in Europe, ensuring wide co-determination coverage.

laws.title: Nachbarschaftsrecht — Neighbour Law (NachbG BW)
laws.subtitle: Tree heights, hedge distances, boundary fences — state-specific rules
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg's Nachbarrechtsgesetz (NachbG BW) governs disputes between neighbours about trees, hedges, fences, and nuisance. Trees must be planted at minimum distances from property boundaries (e.g., high trees: 4m from boundary). Hedges over 2m: special rules apply. Overhanging branches may be cut by the neighbour after notice. Boundary fences: cost shared equally by neighbours. Baden-Württemberg's NachbG BW differs from other states — making it important to consult state-specific rules rather than assuming federal uniformity.
laws.penalty: Violations of planting distances: court order to remove + compensation. Illegal tree removal: up to €50,000.
laws.exceptions: Protected trees (listed trees) require special permit even on private land

quiz.q: What is Germany's neighbour law principle regarding overhanging tree branches?
options: They belong to whoever's land they overhang
The neighbour may cut them after giving notice to the tree owner
They must be removed by the tree owner within 30 days
There is no right to cut overhanging branches
quiz.explanation: German neighbour law generally allows a neighbouring landowner to cut overhanging branches back to the boundary line — but must give the tree owner advance notice and opportunity to do it themselves first.

laws.title: Kündigungsschutz — Employment Protection (KSchG)
laws.subtitle: After 6 months, dismissal requires valid reason; works council must be heard
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Kündigungsschutzgesetz (KSchG) protects employees in firms with more than 10 employees from unfair dismissal after a 6-month probationary period. Valid dismissal reasons are: personal reasons (illness, incapacity), behavioural reasons (gross misconduct), or operational reasons (Betriebsbedingt — restructuring). The works council must be informed before any dismissal — failure to do so makes the dismissal automatically void. Notice periods scale with seniority (4 weeks to 7 months for 20 years' service).
laws.penalty: Unfair dismissal: Arbeitsgericht (Labour Court) order for reinstatement or Abfindung (severance). Dismissing without notice consultation: dismissal automatically void.
laws.exceptions: Firms with 10 or fewer employees have simplified dismissal rules; probationary period (Probezeit) up to 6 months allows dismissal with 2 weeks notice

quiz.q: What must a German employer do before dismissing an employee covered by the KSchG?
options: Inform and consult the works council (Betriebsrat)
Post a public notice of redundancy
quiz.explanation: Under §102 BetrVG, a German employer must inform and consult the Betriebsrat (works council) before any dismissal — failing to do so makes the dismissal automatically void regardless of the underlying reason.

laws.title: Cybercrime — §202a StGB (Ausspähen von Daten)
laws.subtitle: Unauthorised data access: up to 3 years (up to 10 for serious cases)
laws.fullDescription: Germany's computer crime law (§202a StGB — Ausspähen von Daten) criminalises unauthorised access to specially protected data. Related offences: §202b (Abfangen von Daten — intercepting data), §202c (Vorbereitung — preparing hacking tools), §303a/b (data/computer sabotage). Baden-Württemberg's Cyber-Allianz is a public-private partnership protecting companies in the Stuttgart/Karlsruhe tech corridor. The LKA BW operates a dedicated cybercrime unit (ICT crime).
laws.penalty: Data espionage: up to 3 years or fine. Critical infrastructure attacks: up to 10 years. Computer sabotage: up to 10 years.
laws.exceptions: Security researchers with explicit authorisation and coordinated disclosure

quiz.q: What German law criminalises the possession of hacking tools for preparation of cybercrime?
quiz.explanation: §202c StGB (Vorbereitung von Computerkriminalität) criminalises possessing, producing, or distributing tools specifically designed for hacking — even before any actual attack — making preparation itself a criminal offence in Germany.

laws.title: Bürgergeld — Basic Income Support (SGB II)
laws.subtitle: Replaced Hartz IV in 2023; €563/month base (single adult 2024)
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Bürgergeld (SGB II) replaced the controversial Hartz IV system from January 2023. It provides €563/month for a single adult (2024), plus housing costs and health insurance. The system emphasises skills training over immediate job placement. A 2-year grace period prevents authorities from checking assets intensively at the start. Baden-Württemberg's Jobcenter network administers Bürgergeld — the state has above-average employment rates so relatively fewer claimants than some eastern states.
laws.penalty: Refusing suitable employment or training without good reason: benefit reduction up to 30%. Fraud: repayment + prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Those unable to work due to health conditions receive Sozialhilfe (SGB XII) instead
laws.sourceLabel: SGB II — Bürgergeld / Grundsicherung für Arbeitsuchende

quiz.q: What replaced Germany's controversial Hartz IV welfare system in January 2023?
quiz.explanation: Bürgergeld (Citizens' Income) replaced Hartz IV (SGB II) from January 2023, with higher payments, a more trust-based approach to assets, and greater focus on long-term skills training over immediate job placement.

laws.title: Klimaschutz — Climate Protection Act (KSG / KlimaG BW)
laws.subtitle: Baden-Württemberg: climate-neutral by 2040 target
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg's Klimaschutzgesetz (KlimaG BW), amended 2023, sets a binding target of climate neutrality by 2040 — 10 years ahead of Germany's federal 2045 target. Annual CO2 reduction milestones are set by sector (transport, buildings, industry, agriculture). The state has mandatory solar installation for new builds, Moor protection programmes (peatlands sequester CO2), and extensive EV charging infrastructure requirements for new car parks. Companies above certain emissions thresholds must file Klimaschutzbericht (climate progress reports).
laws.penalty: Failure to meet sector targets triggers mandated acceleration measures. Industrial violators of emissions permits: fines up to €500,000.
laws.exceptions: Small businesses under 5 employees exempt from reporting requirements

quiz.q: What year does Baden-Württemberg aim to achieve climate neutrality?
quiz.explanation: Baden-Württemberg's KlimaG BW sets a 2040 climate neutrality target — 5 years earlier than Germany's federal 2045 target — making it one of the most ambitious state-level climate commitments in Europe.

laws.title: Public Smoking — Nichtraucherschutzgesetz BW
laws.subtitle: Smoking banned in most enclosed public spaces
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg's Landesnichtraucherschutzgesetz (LNRSchG BW) bans smoking in restaurants, cafes, bars, public transport, schools, hospitals, and government buildings. Small single-room bars (Eckkneipen) may apply for a smoking licence if under 75m² and adults-only. E-cigarettes and vaping are covered under the same rules in most venues. Baden-Württemberg was one of the stricter southern states in implementing smoking bans — Bavaria went further with a total ban after a 2010 referendum.
laws.penalty: Smoking in prohibited area: €50–€500 fine. Venue allowing illegal smoking: up to €5,000.
laws.exceptions: Designated outdoor smoking areas; specialist tobacco shops; private residences

quiz.q: Which German state held a referendum in 2010 to enforce a total smoking ban in all bars?
quiz.explanation: Bavaria held a referendum in 2010 in which 61% of voters backed a total smoking ban in all Bavarian bars and restaurants — one of the strictest in Germany, and enacted by direct democracy rather than parliament.

laws.title: Führerschein — Driving Licence (FeV)
laws.subtitle: German licence required; EU licences valid; non-EU must convert
laws.fullDescription: EU/EEA driving licences are automatically valid in Germany without conversion. Non-EU licence holders may drive for up to 6 months then must convert (with or without a theory/practical test depending on their country). Germany uses a Fahrerlaubnisklassen system (A, B, C, D, BE etc.) aligned to EU Directive 2006/126. Provisional (L17) driving with an adult supervisor is available at age 17 in Baden-Württemberg — the 'Begleitetes Fahren' programme. The MPU (Medizinisch-Psychologische Untersuchung) is mandatory after serious offences.
laws.penalty: Driving without valid licence: up to 1 year prison or fine. Fraud (using false licence): criminal prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Non-EU licences from countries with bilateral agreements (USA some states, Japan) have simplified conversion

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to participate in Germany's 'Begleitetes Fahren' (supervised driving) programme?
quiz.explanation: Germany's Begleitetes Fahren ab 17 (supervised driving from age 17) allows 17-year-olds to drive accompanied by an approved adult supervisor — giving them road experience before the official licensing age of 18.

laws.title: Angelschein — Fishing Licence (LFischG BW)
laws.subtitle: State fishing licence required; additional water body permit needed
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg requires fishers to hold both a state fishing licence (Staatlicher Angelschein / Fischereischein) — obtained by passing an exam covering fish species, ecology, and regulations — plus a permit for the specific water body (Erlaubnisschein from the riparian rights holder). The Fischereischein is valid for life after passing the exam. The Black Forest and Rhine tributaries are popular trout and grayling fisheries. Catch limits, minimum sizes, and protected seasons (Schonzeiten) apply to each species.
laws.penalty: Fishing without licence: fines up to €5,000. Violating catch limits: fines up to €25,000.
laws.exceptions: Children under 10 may fish with a licensed adult without own licence

quiz.q: What does a German fishing licence (Angelschein) exam test?
options: Knowledge of fish species, ecology, fishing regulations, and conservation
quiz.explanation: Germany's Fischereischein exam tests knowledge of fish species identification, ecological principles, fishing regulations, catch limits, and nature conservation — ensuring anglers understand both the legal and biological aspects of responsible fishing.

laws.title: Jagdgesetz — Hunting Law (BJagdG / LJG BW)
laws.subtitle: Federal and state hunting law; Jagdschein required; fixed seasons
laws.fullDescription: Hunting in Baden-Württemberg is governed by the federal Bundesjagdgesetz (BJagdG) and the state Landesjagdgesetz (LJG BW). A Jagdschein requires passing a comprehensive exam (Jagdprüfung) covering firearms safety, game biology, hunting regulations, and nature protection — often called the 'Grünes Abitur' (Green A-levels) for its difficulty. Fixed hunting seasons (Jagdzeiten) protect animals during breeding; off-season hunting is a criminal offence. Baden-Württemberg has hunting areas (Reviere) leased by hunters from landowners.
laws.penalty: Hunting without licence: up to 2 years or fine. Poaching during closed season: up to 5 years. Illegal methods (traps, lights): up to 5 years.
laws.exceptions: Farmers may take certain wildlife causing crop damage with notification

quiz.q: Why is Germany's hunting licence exam nicknamed the 'Grünes Abitur'?
options: It is as comprehensive and difficult as Germany's school leaving exam
It focuses exclusively on environmental topics
quiz.explanation: The Jagdprüfung (hunting licence exam) is nicknamed 'Grünes Abitur' (Green A-levels) because of its breadth and difficulty — covering game biology, firearms theory and safety, hunting regulations, nature conservation, first aid, and practical shooting tests over an extended preparation period.

laws.title: Infektionsschutz — Infection Control (IfSG)
laws.subtitle: Mandatory reporting of notifiable diseases; isolation powers
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Infektionsschutzgesetz (IfSG) requires mandatory reporting of approximately 50 notifiable diseases (meldepflichtige Krankheiten) by doctors and laboratories to the local health authority (Gesundheitsamt) within 24 hours. The Robert Koch Institut (RKI) compiles national data. Authorities have powers to order quarantine and isolation — these were extensively used during COVID-19. Baden-Württemberg's Gesundheitsämter operate under state Health Ministry supervision. Vaccination records must be maintained and may be checked for certain activities.
laws.penalty: Non-reporting by medical professionals: fines up to €25,000. Violating quarantine orders: up to 2 years or fine.
laws.exceptions: Doctors have patient confidentiality rights balanced against reporting obligations — anonymised reporting is permitted in some cases

quiz.q: Which federal body compiles Germany's national notifiable disease data?
quiz.explanation: The Robert Koch Institut (RKI) is Germany's central public health authority, compiling notifiable disease surveillance data submitted by Gesundheitsämter across all 16 states. It was central to Germany's COVID-19 response.

laws.title: Einkommensteuer — Income Tax (EStG)
laws.subtitle: Progressive 0–45%; Solidaritätszuschlag largely abolished
laws.fullDescription: Germany's income tax (Einkommensteuer — EStG) is progressive: 0% up to the Grundfreibetrag (€11,604 in 2024), then rising from 14% to 42% for most incomes, with a 45% Spitzensteuersatz (top rate) on income above ~€277,826. The Solidaritätszuschlag (solidarity surcharge), originally to fund reunification, was abolished for 90% of taxpayers in 2021 but remains for top earners. Baden-Württemberg's Finanzämter administer tax collection. Tax returns (Steuererklärung) are due July 31 (or with a tax adviser: February 28 of the following year).
laws.penalty: Late filing: surcharge up to 10% of tax owed. Tax evasion: up to 10 years prison. Large-scale evasion (>€1 million): mandatory prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Married couples may use Ehegattensplitting (income splitting) reducing overall tax burden

quiz.q: What is Germany's top income tax rate (Spitzensteuersatz)?
quiz.explanation: Germany's Spitzensteuersatz (top income tax rate) is 45%, applied to taxable income above approximately €277,826/year. The standard top rate of 42% applies from around €66,761 — making Germany's middle-income tax burden among Europe's highest.

laws.title: Verfassungsrecht — Baden-Württemberg State Constitution
laws.subtitle: BW Landesverfassung 1953; state parliament, courts, rights
laws.fullDescription: Baden-Württemberg was formed in 1952 from three former states (Baden, Württemberg-Baden, Württemberg-Hohenzollern) — confirmed by referendum. Its Landesverfassung (State Constitution) of 1953 establishes the Landtag (state parliament, 120+ seats, 5-year terms), Ministerrat (cabinet), and State Constitutional Court (Staatsgerichtshof). Article 2 guarantees the right to work. Baden-Württemberg is one of Germany's wealthiest states with the 3rd highest GDP. The CDU governed for 58 consecutive years (1953–2011) before losing to the Greens.
laws.penalty: Violations of constitutional rights: judicial review by Staatsgerichtshof BW or Federal Constitutional Court
laws.exceptions: State constitution may not contradict the federal Grundgesetz — federal law prevails in conflict

quiz.q: How was Baden-Württemberg created in 1952?
options: By merging three former German states confirmed by referendum
quiz.explanation: Baden-Württemberg was created on 25 April 1952 by merging Baden, Württemberg-Baden, and Württemberg-Hohenzollern — the merger was confirmed by a referendum in which voters chose a unified state over re-establishing the original separate states.

laws.title: Parking Rules — StVO §12
laws.subtitle: No parking at bus stops, crossings, or within 5m of junctions
laws.fullDescription: Germany's StVO §12 sets comprehensive no-parking rules: at bus stops (15m radius), pedestrian crossings, within 5m of junctions, on cycle paths, on tram lines, and opposite another vehicle if road width would be insufficient. Baden-Württemberg cities like Stuttgart (with its hilly terrain) have extensive Anwohnerparken (resident parking zones) — residents pay ~€30/year for a zone permit, while visitors pay €1–3/hour. Illegal parking tickets start at €10 and can include towing (Abschleppen) at the driver's expense (€150–€300).
laws.penalty: Parking at bus stop: €25. Parking on cycle path: €55. Causing danger: €70. Towing costs: €150–€300 at driver's expense.
laws.exceptions: Loading/unloading within 3 minutes with hazard lights; disabled badge holders have extended rights

quiz.q: What is the no-parking radius around bus stops in Germany?
quiz.explanation: Germany's StVO §12 prohibits parking within 15 metres of a bus stop sign — ensuring buses can pull in and passengers can board safely without obstruction.

laws.title: Bodenschutz — Soil Protection (BBodSchG)
laws.subtitle: Contaminated land must be investigated and remediated
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Federal Soil Protection Act (BBodSchG) imposes obligations on landowners to investigate and remediate contaminated soil. Baden-Württemberg, with its industrial history (chemicals, automotive), has many altlastenverdächtige Flächen (potentially contaminated sites). The state's LUBW (environmental agency) maintains contaminated site registers. Former petrol stations, industrial sites, and dry cleaners are particularly monitored. Responsibility for remediation can extend to previous owners.
laws.penalty: Failure to remediate when ordered: fines up to €50,000 + enforced remediation at owner's cost. Deliberate contamination: criminal prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Naturally occurring background levels of metals don't trigger remediation obligations

quiz.q: Who is responsible for soil contamination remediation under German law?
options: The person who caused the contamination (Verursacher); if unavailable, the current owner
quiz.explanation: Germany's BBodSchG establishes a liability hierarchy: first the Verursacher (polluter who caused the contamination); if they cannot be found, the Gesamtrechtsnachfolger (legal successor); and finally the current landowner — implementing a strict polluter-pays principle.

laws.title: Körperverletzung — Assault (§223 StGB)
laws.subtitle: Physical assault: up to 5 years; serious assault: up to 10 years
laws.fullDescription: Germany's assault law (§223 StGB — Körperverletzung) covers intentional or negligent physical harm. Simple assault: up to 5 years or fine. Gefährliche Körperverletzung (dangerous assault — using weapon, gang attack): up to 10 years. Schwere Körperverletzung (serious injury — loss of limb, eye, serious deformity): up to 10 years. Fahrlässige Körperverletzung (negligent bodily harm): up to 3 years. Self-defence (Notwehr §32 StGB) is a complete defence if proportionate.
laws.penalty: Simple assault: up to 5 years or fine. Gang assault or weapon use: 6 months to 10 years. Serious injury: 1–10 years.
laws.exceptions: Self-defence (Notwehr) — force must be proportionate to the threat

quiz.q: What is the German legal term for assault with a weapon or in a group?
quiz.explanation: Gefährliche Körperverletzung (§224 StGB — dangerous bodily harm) applies when assault involves a weapon, a dangerous instrument, ambush, joint action of multiple persons, or methods endangering life — carrying 6 months to 10 years.

laws.title: Schuldrecht — Contract Law (BGB §241ff)
laws.subtitle: Contracts binding without writing in most cases; pacta sunt servanda
laws.fullDescription: German contract law (BGB §241ff — Schuldrecht) follows the principle that contracts are binding once offer and acceptance meet, usually without requiring writing. However, certain contracts require notarisation: real estate sales (§311b BGB), marriage contracts, GmbH formation, and inheritance waivers. German courts enforce contracts strictly but have consumer protection exceptions. General Terms and Conditions (AGB — Allgemeine Geschäftsbedingungen) are subject to content review under §305ff BGB — surprising or unfair clauses may be struck down.
laws.penalty: Breach of contract: damages (Schadensersatz), specific performance (Erfüllung), or contract termination (Rücktritt).
laws.exceptions: Contracts under §138 BGB that are grossly immoral or usurious are void

quiz.q: Which types of contracts in Germany require notarisation?
options: Real estate sales, marriage contracts, and GmbH formation
quiz.explanation: German law requires notarisation (notarielle Beurkundung) for real estate transactions (BGB §311b), marriage property agreements, GmbH share transfers, and inheritance waivers — ensuring that parties to major legal acts understand the consequences.

laws.title: BAföG — Student Financial Aid (BAföG)
laws.subtitle: 50% grant, 50% loan; repayable up to €10,010 maximum
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Bundesausbildungsförderungsgesetz (BAföG) provides means-tested financial support to students in higher education and vocational training. Half is a grant (not repayable); half is an interest-free loan, with a maximum repayment of €10,010 regardless of total received. Baden-Württemberg has some of Germany's top universities (Heidelberg, Tübingen, KIT Karlsruhe, Stuttgart) and a high number of BAföG recipients. The 2022 reform raised the rates and parent income thresholds to reach more students. Applications go to Studentenwerke.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent BAföG claims: immediate repayment of all funds + prosecution.
laws.exceptions: Students from wealthy families (above income thresholds) do not qualify

quiz.q: What is the maximum amount a German BAföG loan recipient must repay, regardless of how much they received?
quiz.explanation: Germany's BAföG loan repayment is capped at €10,010 — meaning that even if a student received €30,000 in loans, they only repay €10,010. This cap makes higher education financially accessible while keeping loan risk manageable.

laws.title: Mietspiegel — Rent Index (BGB §558c)
laws.subtitle: Published rent index used to challenge rent increases in cities
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Mietspiegel (rent index) is published by municipalities and reflects average rents paid for comparable properties in an area. Landlords wishing to raise rent in areas with housing shortage must demonstrate the new rent doesn't exceed 10% above the Mietspiegel comparable. In Baden-Württemberg, Stuttgart and Freiburg publish detailed Mietspiegel. The Mietpreisbremse (rent brake — BGB §556d) caps initial rents in designated high-demand areas at max 10% above the local Mietspiegel.
laws.penalty: Rent increases beyond Mietspiegel limits: tenant may refuse excess; court orders excess repayment.
laws.exceptions: New constructions and comprehensive renovations are often exempt from rent brake

quiz.q: What is the maximum percentage above the local Mietspiegel that the rent brake allows for new tenancies?
quiz.explanation: Germany's Mietpreisbremse (BGB §556d) caps new tenancy rents at a maximum of 10% above the local Mietspiegel (rent index) in designated high-demand areas — protecting tenants from rent spikes when moving.

laws.title: Cookie Consent — DSGVO/TTDSG
laws.subtitle: Websites must obtain consent for non-essential cookies
laws.fullDescription: Under Germany's Telecommunications and Telemedia Data Protection Act (TTDSG) and GDPR, websites serving German users must obtain informed, specific, and freely given consent before setting non-essential cookies (analytics, advertising, tracking). The 'consent or pay' model (where users pay or consent) has been under scrutiny by German DPAs. The DSGVO's requirement for freely given consent means cookie walls (blocking access without consent) are generally illegal. Baden-Württemberg's LfDI has investigated numerous websites.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant cookie practices: GDPR fines up to €20 million or 4% of global turnover. Consumer associations can also sue under UWG.
laws.exceptions: Strictly necessary cookies (login sessions, shopping carts) don't require consent

quiz.q: Under German law, what type of cookies require user consent?
quiz.explanation: Germany's TTDSG and GDPR require consent for any non-essential cookies — including analytics (like Google Analytics), advertising pixels, and social media tracking. Only strictly necessary cookies (session management, security) may be set without consent.

laws.title: Namensrecht — Name Law (BGB §1355)
laws.subtitle: Both partners may take shared name; hyphenated names allowed
laws.fullDescription: Under BGB §1355, married couples in Germany choose a shared family name (Ehename) — either partner's name or a hyphenated combination. Children normally receive the Ehename; if no Ehename is chosen, parents choose the child's surname at birth. First name rules (Vornamensrecht) require names to clearly indicate gender, not be a surname, and not endanger the child's wellbeing — the Standesamt can reject inappropriate names. Famous rejections include 'Lucifer', 'Hitler', and various trademarked names.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent name use: criminal impersonation. Standesamt refusal of name: administrative appeal to courts.
laws.exceptions: Artists and performers may use stage names (Künstlername) without legal change

quiz.q: Can German parents give their child any name they choose?
options: No — the Standesamt may reject names that don't indicate gender, are surnames, or could harm the child
Only names from an approved list
quiz.explanation: Germany's Standesamt (civil registry) can reject baby names that: don't clearly indicate gender, are surnames, are ridiculous or offensive, or could harm the child's wellbeing. This gives Germany one of Europe's more restrictive name-choice regimes.

laws.title: Luftqualität — Air Quality (BImSchG / 39. BImSchV)
laws.subtitle: Air pollution limits; diesel driving bans in polluted cities
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Federal Immission Control Act (BImSchG) and EU Air Quality Directive (39. BImSchV) set binding limits for PM10, PM2.5, NO2, and ozone. Stuttgart — located in a valley with poor air circulation — historically had Germany's highest urban NO2 levels. The Stuttgart Umweltzone (environmental zone) bans vehicles without at least a Euro 4 petrol or Euro 6 diesel engine. Feinstaubalarm (fine particle alert) is declared on days with forecast pollution peaks, with voluntary measures.
laws.penalty: Driving in Umweltzone without valid badge: €80 fine. Exceeding industrial emission permits: fines up to €50,000.
laws.exceptions: Emergency vehicles; vehicles with disability adaptations; certain vintage vehicles

quiz.q: Why does Stuttgart have Germany's worst urban air quality problems?
options: Valley location with poor air circulation trapping pollutants
quiz.explanation: Stuttgart sits in a basin surrounded by hills that prevent wind from dispersing pollutants — making it Germany's most air-polluted city despite having a smaller population than cities like Berlin, Hamburg, or Munich. This geography prompted Germany's first diesel driving bans.

laws.title: Gambling Law — GlüStV 2021
laws.subtitle: Online gambling newly regulated; sports betting licensed; land-based casinos state-regulated
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Glücksspielstaatsvertrag 2021 (GlüStV 2021) regulates gambling across all 16 states. Baden-Württemberg operates state casinos (Spielbanken) in Baden-Baden, Konstanz, and Stuttgart. Online casino gambling was technically illegal until 2021 when the new GlüStV created a federal licensing framework. Sports betting requires a licence. Slot machines (Geldspielgeräte) in pubs are regulated by the Spielverordnung — limited to 3 machines per venue. Gambling addiction resources are legally mandated.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed gambling: criminal prosecution. Tax evasion on gambling winnings: back-tax + fines. Under-18 access to gambling: licence revocation.
laws.exceptions: Lottery (LOTTO), scratch cards, and horse racing have separate licensing frameworks

quiz.q: In which Baden-Württemberg city is there a famous historical casino?
quiz.explanation: Baden-Baden's Spielbank (casino) is one of Europe's most famous and historic casinos — opened in 1838, it was frequented by Dostoyevsky (who wrote 'The Gambler' based on his experiences there), Kaiser Wilhelm II, and numerous European royals.

laws.title: Transplantationsgesetz — Organ Donation Law
laws.subtitle: Germany switched to opt-out (double opt-out) system in 2022
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Transplantationsgesetz (TPG) was amended to create a 'double opt-out' system effective 2022. All residents are presumed to be organ donors unless they register their refusal in the national register (Organspenderegister) or their family objects at time of death. Families retain a decisive role — they can override the presumed consent even without a documented objection. Baden-Württemberg hospitals are active transplant centres. Germany historically had Europe's largest gap between organ needs and donations; the reform aimed to address this.
laws.penalty: Illegal organ trading: up to 5 years. Transplant manipulation: up to 10 years (following a 2012 scandal).
laws.exceptions: Religious objections and conscientious opt-outs: full right to register refusal at any time

quiz.q: What organ donation system did Germany adopt in 2022?
quiz.explanation: Germany switched to a 'double opt-out' (Widerspruchlösung) system in 2022 — all residents are presumed to consent to organ donation unless they register an objection in the national register. Families retain the right to override presumed consent.

laws.title: Wohnungseigentumsgesetz — Condominium Law (WEG)
laws.subtitle: Apartment owners have shared liability for common areas
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Wohnungseigentumsgesetz (WEG) governs jointly owned apartment buildings (Wohnungseigentümergemeinschaft — WEG). Each owner has individual title to their flat plus a share of common areas (Gemeinschaftseigentum). Annual general meetings (Eigentümerversammlung) vote on building management, maintenance budgets, and major repairs. The 2020 WEG reform made it easier to pass resolutions for energy efficiency improvements and EV charging points. Baden-Württemberg's Stuttgart has many WEG properties in its compact urban areas.
laws.penalty: Failure to pay WEG fees (Hausgeld): enforcement + potential forced sale. Obstructing building measures lawfully passed: court injunction.
laws.exceptions: Individual flat modifications require WEG approval if affecting common structures

quiz.q: What is the German term for the annual meeting of apartment owners in a jointly owned building?
quiz.explanation: The Eigentümerversammlung (owners' assembly) is the annual meeting of all flat owners in a Wohnungseigentümergemeinschaft (WEG) — where they vote on maintenance works, set the budget (Haushaltsplan), and elect the building manager (Verwalter).

laws.title: Berufsausbildung — Apprenticeship System (BBiG)
laws.subtitle: Germany's dual system: company training + Berufsschule
laws.fullDescription: Germany's dual vocational training system (duales Ausbildungssystem) is globally admired. Under the Berufsbildungsgesetz (BBiG), apprentices (Auszubildende — Azubis) spend 3–4 days/week in a company and 1–2 days in Berufsschule (vocational school). Duration: 2–3.5 years. Completion confers a recognised Berufsabschluss (vocational qualification). Baden-Württemberg has training programmes in automotive engineering (Daimler, Porsche), IT (SAP), and precision manufacturing (Bosch). Minimum apprentice pay is €620/month (1st year, 2024) rising annually.
laws.penalty: Employers not fulfilling training obligations: regulatory action by IHK/HWK. Breach of apprenticeship contract: compensation.
laws.exceptions: University graduates may still do apprenticeships; dual study programmes combine both Ausbildung and degree

quiz.q: What is Germany's vocational training system called?
quiz.explanation: Germany's duales Ausbildungssystem (dual vocational training system) combines workplace training at a company with theoretical education at a Berufsschule — the model has been adopted internationally and is considered a key reason for Germany's low youth unemployment.

laws.title: Tierhaltung — Livestock and Pet Regulations (TierSchG)
laws.subtitle: Factory farming standards; livestock welfare; pet registration
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Tierschutzgesetz sets minimum standards for livestock farming — space requirements for pigs, chickens, and cattle that are among Europe's highest under the Nutztierhaltungsverordnungen. Battery cages for hens were banned in Germany in 2010. Baden-Württemberg's agricultural areas (Schwäbisch Hall, Hohenlohe) have traditional livestock farming. Importation of cats and dogs from non-EU countries requires microchip, rabies vaccination, and tapeworm treatment. Exotic pets (listed species) require CITES documentation.
laws.penalty: Factory farming violations: fines up to €25,000 + farm closure. Cruel treatment of livestock: up to 3 years prison. Illegal exotic pet import: confiscation + fines.
laws.exceptions: Research institutions with approved ethics review may hold animals under special conditions

quiz.q: When did Germany ban battery cages for laying hens?
quiz.explanation: Germany banned conventional battery cages for laying hens in 2010, ahead of the EU-wide ban in 2012. The German ban was even stricter — also phasing out 'enriched cages' that the EU still allows.

laws.title: Fahrerflucht — Hit and Run (§142 StGB)
laws.subtitle: Leaving accident scene without waiting or reporting: up to 3 years
laws.fullDescription: Under §142 StGB, a driver involved in an accident must remain at the scene until the police or injured parties can record their details — or report within 24 hours if no one is present. Leaving the scene (Fahrerflucht) is a criminal offence, not merely a traffic violation. Baden-Württemberg police use CCTV and witness networks intensively to identify Fahrerflucht offenders. Even minor parking damage followed by leaving without a note can trigger prosecution if the victim reports it.
laws.penalty: Fahrerflucht after accident with personal injury: up to 3 years or fine + licence revocation. Damage only: up to 3 years or fine.
laws.exceptions: Emergency situations where driver must get help immediately — but must report to police as soon as possible

quiz.q: If you damage a parked car in Germany and the owner is not present, what must you do?
options: Drive away — minor damage doesn't count
Leave a note and wait at least 30 minutes, then report to police if no one comes
Call police immediately from the scene
