Pay a fixed fee to a damage fund
quiz.explanation: German law (§142 StGB) requires a driver who damages a parked car to wait a reasonable time (typically at least 30 minutes), leave contact details if the owner doesn't appear, and report to the police. Failure to do this is Fahrerflucht — a criminal offence.

laws.title: Integrationsgesetz — Integration Law (IntG)
laws.subtitle: Language courses and civic education mandatory for some asylum seekers
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Integration Act (Integrationsgesetz) requires asylum seekers with good prospects of staying to attend Integrationskurse (integration courses) — German language training to level B1 plus civic orientation. Baden-Württemberg's BAMF-approved integration course providers are concentrated in Stuttgart, Freiburg, and Mannheim. Refusal to attend without good reason leads to reduced benefits. The state also runs its own WABE programme (Wege in Ausbildung, Beschäftigung — pathways to training and employment).
laws.penalty: Non-attendance of mandatory courses: Bürgergeld/Sozialleistung reduction up to 30%. Fraudulent asylum claims: deportation + ban.
laws.exceptions: Those exempted: elderly, seriously ill, carers of young children

quiz.q: What level of German language is the integration course designed to achieve?
quiz.explanation: Germany's integration course language component is designed to bring participants to B1 level (intermediate) on the Common European Framework of Reference — enough to handle everyday situations, simple work tasks, and civic participation.

laws.title: Sportrecht — Sports and Liability (BGB / NSSG)
laws.subtitle: Sports injuries during proper play: reduced liability; doping banned
laws.fullDescription: In German sports law, participants in contact sports accept inherent risks of injury within the rules — reducing liability for within-rules incidents. However, deliberate foul play causing injury triggers full civil and criminal liability. Anti-doping in Germany is governed by the Anti-Doping-Gesetz (AntiDopG) — possession of performance-enhancing drugs for self-doping became criminal in 2015, not just for elite athletes. Baden-Württemberg hosts major sporting events (Stuttgart's Mercedes-Benz Arena; the 2006 World Cup games in Stuttgart).
laws.penalty: Deliberate sports violence: §223ff StGB prosecution. Doping for competitive advantage: up to 10 years prison. Sports fraud (match-fixing): §265c StGB, up to 5 years.
laws.exceptions: Normal contact within rules of the sport; accidental injury without negligence

quiz.q: What did Germany criminalise in 2015 regarding doping that went beyond previous anti-doping rules?
options: Athletes' personal/recreational doping (self-doping) even in amateur sport
quiz.explanation: Germany's 2015 Anti-Doping-Gesetz criminalised self-doping by athletes — making it illegal for athletes (not just suppliers) to possess or use doping substances even for personal use in competitive sport. This applied to amateur and professional athletes alike.

laws.title: IT-Sicherheitsgesetz — IT Security Law (BSIG)
laws.subtitle: Critical infrastructure operators must report cyber incidents
laws.fullDescription: Germany's IT Security Act (IT-SiG 2.0, 2021) updated the BSI Act (BSIG) — requiring critical infrastructure operators (KRITIS — energy, water, transport, health, finance, digital) to implement minimum cybersecurity measures and report significant incidents to the BSI (Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik) within 24 hours. Companies of 'particular public interest' (large manufacturers, defence industry) face additional requirements. Baden-Württemberg's car manufacturers and Bosch are designated KRITIS operators.
laws.penalty: KRITIS operators failing to implement minimum measures: fines up to €20 million. Non-reporting of incidents: up to €10 million.
laws.exceptions: Academic research networks and small businesses excluded from KRITIS designation

quiz.q: Within how many hours must German critical infrastructure operators report cybersecurity incidents?
quiz.explanation: Germany's BSIG (IT Security Act) requires critical infrastructure (KRITIS) operators to report significant cybersecurity incidents to the BSI within 24 hours of detection — enabling early warning and coordinated response across sectors.

laws.title: Hochwasserschutz — Flood Protection (WHG)
laws.subtitle: Flood zones restrict development; property owners have preparedness duties
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Wasserhaushaltsgesetz (WHG) §§ 72-81 establishes flood protection zones (Überschwemmungsgebiete) with varying degrees of restriction on development and activity. In designated 100-year flood zones, construction of new buildings is generally prohibited. Baden-Württemberg has extensive Rhine Valley flood plains — the 2021 European floods caused significant damage. Property owners in flood zones must take individual preparedness measures. The state's Hochwassermeldedienst provides real-time flood alerts.
laws.penalty: Building in prohibited flood zones: demolition orders + fines up to €50,000. Failure to maintain protective flood barriers: civil liability.
laws.exceptions: Emergency infrastructure (flood barriers, pump stations) may be located in flood zones

quiz.q: What construction is generally prohibited in designated 100-year flood zones in Germany?
options: Any new residential or commercial buildings
quiz.explanation: In designated 100-year flood zones (Überschwemmungsgebiete) in Germany, constructing new buildings is generally prohibited — protecting both future occupants and the flood retention capacity of the floodplain. Existing buildings may be retained but face restrictions.

laws.title: Pflegeversicherung — Long-Term Care Insurance (SGB XI)
laws.subtitle: Mandatory for all insured; 5 care grades; up to €3,386/month
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Pflegeversicherung (long-term care insurance — SGB XI) is compulsory for all health-insured persons. Contribution: ~3.4% of gross salary (3.6% for childless workers over 23). Care is assessed in 5 Pflegegrade (care grades 1–5) by the Medizinischer Dienst (MD). Grade 5 (most dependent): up to €3,386/month for in-home care, more for nursing home costs (with co-payments). Baden-Württemberg has a large network of private and public care homes. Relatives providing informal care receive pension credits.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent care grade claims: repayment + prosecution. Care facilities providing below-standard care: closure by Heimaufsicht.
laws.exceptions: Those providing informal home care can receive Pflegegeld (cash benefit: €332–€901/month) to compensate family carers

quiz.q: How many care grades exist in Germany's long-term care system?
quiz.explanation: Germany's SGB XI Pflegeversicherung uses 5 Pflegegrade (care grades) from Grade 1 (minor impairments) to Grade 5 (most severe dependence, often including dementia). The grade determines the level of benefits — from advisory visits to full nursing home support.

laws.title: Pressefreiheit — Press Freedom (Art. 5 GG)
laws.subtitle: Press freedom constitutionally guaranteed; editorial secrecy protected
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Basic Law Article 5 guarantees press freedom (Pressefreiheit) and freedom of expression (Meinungsfreiheit). The press may not be censored. Journalists have a right to protect their sources (Zeugnisverweigerungsrecht). Police may not search newsrooms without extraordinary judicial authorisation — the constitutional protection of editorial secrecy is strong. Baden-Württemberg is home to major media (Stuttgarter Zeitung, SWR broadcaster). Germany ranked 11th globally for press freedom in 2024 (RSF index).
laws.penalty: State interference with press: unconstitutional — Art. 5 GG. Defamation by press: §186ff StGB (Beleidigung/Verleumdung). Revenue from press advertising not separately taxed.
laws.exceptions: Press freedom is not absolute — incitement to hatred, defamation, and state secrets law still apply

quiz.q: What is Germany's constitutional provision protecting press freedom?
quiz.explanation: Article 5 of Germany's Grundgesetz (Basic Law) guarantees freedom of expression (Meinungsfreiheit) and freedom of the press (Pressefreiheit) — with exceptions for laws protecting honour, youth protection, and personal rights. It prohibits censorship explicitly.

laws.title: Schönheitsreparaturen — Cosmetic Repair Clauses (BGB)
laws.subtitle: Standard lease clauses requiring tenant redecoration often invalid
laws.fullDescription: German courts have repeatedly struck down standard tenancy clauses requiring tenants to repaint and redecorate at the end of a tenancy (Schönheitsreparaturklauseln) if they set fixed intervals regardless of actual condition, or if the flat was handed over unrenovated. Baden-Württemberg's Mieterbund (tenant association) provides advice on which clauses are enforceable. Landlords must prove the flat was in renovated condition at the start if they want renovation at the end.
laws.penalty: Invalid clauses: tenant not obliged to redecorate. Valid clauses: tenant must return flat in acceptable decorative condition. Disputes: Amtsgericht (local court).
laws.exceptions: Both sides can always negotiate a specific agreement about the decoration condition

quiz.q: Are all tenancy clauses requiring tenants to repaint walls valid in Germany?
options: Yes — all tenancy terms are binding once signed
No — courts have invalidated many standard redecoration clauses as unfair
Only if the landlord also painted before the tenancy
quiz.explanation: Germany's BGH (Federal Court of Justice) has repeatedly invalidated standard tenancy redecoration clauses — especially those with fixed time intervals (e.g., 'repaint every 3 years') regardless of actual condition, or where the flat was handed over unrenovated.

laws.title: Diebstahl — Theft (§242 StGB)
laws.subtitle: Theft of any property: up to 5 years; shoplifting follows same law
laws.fullDescription: Germany's theft law (§242 StGB — Diebstahl) covers taking another's moveable property with intent to keep it. There is no separate shoplifting offence — all theft falls under §242. Schwerer Diebstahl (aggravated theft — §243) covers theft from secure locations, theft of sacred objects, or professional theft: up to 10 years. Räuberischer Diebstahl (§252) — using violence after theft to keep the goods — bridges theft and robbery. Baden-Württemberg's retail associations have sophisticated RFID systems.
laws.penalty: Simple theft: up to 5 years or fine. Aggravated theft (§243): 3 months to 10 years. Robbery (§249): 1–15 years.
laws.exceptions: Petty theft (Bagatelldiebstahl) — no separate category; all theft prosecutable though prosecutors may exercise Opportunitätsprinzip

quiz.q: Is shoplifting treated as a separate, lesser offence in Germany?
options: Yes — fines only for first offence under €50
No — all theft falls under §242 StGB with the same potential penalty
quiz.explanation: Germany has no separate 'shoplifting' category — all theft, however small, falls under §242 StGB (Diebstahl) with a potential maximum of 5 years imprisonment, though prosecutors use discretion (Opportunitätsprinzip) not to prosecute truly trivial cases.

laws.title: Grundgesetz — Germany's Basic Law (Art. 1–20)
laws.subtitle: Human dignity inviolable; federal democratic state; welfare state
laws.fullDescription: Germany's Grundgesetz (Basic Law, 1949) is the federal constitution with special protections. Art. 1: Human dignity is inviolable — no law may override it. Art. 2: Personal liberty. Art. 3: Equality before law. Art. 5: Free speech/press. Art. 8: Assembly. Art. 9: Association. Art. 20: Eternal Clause — Germany is a democratic, federal, social state (cannot be changed even by unanimous vote). Art. 79(3): Eternity Clause — Art. 1 and 20 cannot be amended at all. Baden-Württemberg's state constitution must comply with the Grundgesetz.
laws.penalty: Violations of basic rights: Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) review. Unconstitutional laws: struck down.
laws.exceptions: Art. 79(3) Ewigkeitsklausel: Art. 1 (dignity) and Art. 20 (democracy/federalism) are permanently unamendable

quiz.q: Which provision of Germany's Basic Law makes human dignity and democracy permanently unamendable?
quiz.explanation: Art. 79(3) GG — the Ewigkeitsklausel (Eternity Clause) — makes Arts. 1 (human dignity) and 20 (democratic, federal, social state) permanently unamendable. Even a unanimous Bundestag and Bundesrat vote cannot touch these provisions — a direct lesson from the Weimar Republic's collapse.

laws.title: Stuttgart 21 — Germany's Largest Rail Project (Unique to BW)
laws.subtitle: €10bn+ tunnel project replacing Stuttgart's terminus station
laws.fullDescription: Stuttgart 21 is Germany's most controversial infrastructure project — a €10+ billion project to convert Stuttgart's historic terminus station (Kopfbahnhof) into an underground through-station, freeing surface land for development. Construction began 2010 after massive protests (Montagsdemos — Monday demonstrations, Schlichtung mediation led by Heiner Geißler). The Federal Administrative Court repeatedly upheld the project. Expected completion: 2025–2026. The project doubled in cost from original estimates. Baden-Württemberg's state government funds a share alongside Deutsche Bahn AG and the federal government.
laws.penalty: Trespassing on construction sites: immediate arrest + civil liability. Protest blocking access routes: assembly law intervention.
laws.exceptions: The public mediation (Schlichtung) process — a German-pioneered method of structured civic dialogue — was watched globally

quiz.q: What unique democratic process was used to mediate the Stuttgart 21 controversy?
options: A televised Schlichtung (mediation/arbitration) process under an independent facilitator
quiz.explanation: Stuttgart 21's Schlichtung was a groundbreaking 9-session public mediation process in 2010, televised live, with project opponents and proponents presenting arguments before mediator Heiner Geißler — a model of structured civic dialogue later referenced in democratic process reform discussions globally.
